name: HCG and clomiphene for voice

lead: hCG and clomiphene are prescription drugs that raise the body's own testosterone, used for fertility and, off-label, for male low testosterone. Forum users mention them hoping higher testosterone will deepen or maintain a lower voice.

hCG mimics luteinizing hormone and stimulates the testes to make testosterone. Clomiphene blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH, LH and FSH release. Encyclopedic sources describe no effect on adult voice pitch, and no published studies have tested either drug for voice. Voice deepening from testosterone is associated with puberty, and the laryngeal changes of puberty are generally described as lasting.

paras: Both are prescribed by clinicians for fertility or hypogonadism, with blood-test monitoring. Voice is not a prescribed use.

Clomiphene can cause visual disturbances, headaches and hot flashes, and hCG carries cautions for several conditions. Both are prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and are banned in competitive sport.

angle.text: hCG and clomiphene are prescription drugs that raise the body's own testosterone, and forum users mention them hoping for a deeper voice. Both are used for fertility and off-label for male hypogonadism; no studies address voice.

lead: In looksmaxxing discussion, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and clomiphene (clomifene) are two prescription drugs sometimes mentioned as ways of raising endogenous testosterone, with the idea that higher testosterone could deepen or maintain a lower voice. Both are used medically for fertility and, off-label, for male hypogonadism.[1][2]

hCG is a hormone that resembles luteinizing hormone and stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to make testosterone.[2] Clomiphene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH, FSH and LH release.[1] Encyclopedic sources on both drugs do not describe an effect on adult voice pitch.[1][2]
No clinical studies of either drug for voice were found. The voice-deepening effect of testosterone is associated with puberty, and the larynx changes of puberty are generally described as lasting.
infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia[1]
Both appear on anti-doping prohibited lists[1][2]

paras: Clomiphene was synthesised by Merrell chemists in 1956 and approved in the US in 1967 for inducing ovulation in women. It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] It is also used off-label in men with low testosterone, and the enclomifene isomer alone is reported to raise testosterone about twice as effectively as the mixture.[1]
Reported adverse effects include visual disturbances, headaches, hot flashes and abdominal discomfort; rarer effects include liver inflammation, raised triglycerides and hair loss.[1]

hCG is made by placental cells and is used clinically to treat certain forms of hypogonadism, to maintain fertility and testicular size in men on testosterone therapy, and to trigger ovulation.[2] Prolonged use in males can increase androgen production, and caution is advised in people with heart failure, hypertension, kidney dysfunction, migraines or epilepsy.[2] In the 1970s the FDA required a disclaimer on hCG weight-loss advertising, and in 2011 banned over-the-counter hCG diet products.[2]

Proponents in appearance communities reason that raising endogenous testosterone while avoiding testosterone replacement could support a deeper voice. The Wikipedia articles on both drugs list fertility, hypogonadism and testicular function as the uses and do not mention voice effects.[1][2] No published trial was identified that measured vocal pitch or resonance in adults after either drug.
Both drugs require a prescription in the US, UK and Australia, and both appear on anti-doping lists; several athletes have been sanctioned for hCG.[1][2]
